reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles
chapter_title: Description of Continuous Flight Auger Pile Types and Basic Mechanisms

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: CFA piles are drilled to final depth in one continuous process with a continuous flight auger whose soil-filled flights support the hole; concrete or sand/cement grout is pumped through the hollow stem as the auger is withdrawn, and reinforcement is placed in the fluid concrete/grout. Typical diameters 0.3 to 0.9 m (12 to 36 in.), lengths up to 30 m (100 ft).
sections.body: CFA piles are a type of drilled foundation drilled to final depth in one continuous process with a continuous flight auger (Figure 2.1). While drilling, the auger flights fill with soil, providing lateral support and stability (Figure 2.2a); as the auger is withdrawn, concrete or sand/cement grout is pumped through the hollow center of the auger pipe to its base (Figure 2.2b), so the hole is continuously supported; reinforcement is placed into the fluid concrete/grout immediately after withdrawal (Figure 2.2c). Typical diameters are 0.3 to 0.9 m (12 to 36 in.) and lengths up to 30 m (100 ft); U.S. practice has tended toward 0.3 to 0.6 m (12 to 24 in.) because less powerful rigs were used, European practice toward larger diameters [up to 1.5 m (60 in.)], and recent U.S. use toward 0.6 to 0.9 m (24 to 36 in.). Reinforcement is often confined to the upper 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft), where bending stresses are transferred; full-length reinforcement is sometimes used. CFA piles are used as single piles (soundwall or light pole foundations) or, for bridges and large structures, in groups with a cap like driven piles (Figures 2.3 and 2.4); typical minimum center-to-center spacing is 3 to 5 diameters (p. 4). Compared with drilled shafts, casing or slurry is avoided and drilling is faster, but the torque demand is high, so diameters and lengths are generally smaller, and CFA piles are limited to soil or very weak rock. Compared with driven piles, noise and vibration are minimized, splices and cutoffs are eliminated and heave is avoided with non-displacement piles; but QA methods to verify structural integrity and bearing capacity are less reliable, and spoils must be collected and disposed of (a significant issue for contaminated soils or limited site room) (p. 6). (pp. 3 to 6)
key_points: Pile drilled in one continuous process; soil-filled flights support the hole (p. 3).
Grout/concrete pumped through the hollow stem during withdrawal; rebar placed in fluid grout (p. 3).
Diameters 0.3 to 0.9 m (12 to 36 in.), lengths up to 30 m (100 ft); Europe up to 1.5 m (60 in.) (p. 4).
Reinforcement often confined to the upper 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft) (p. 4).
Typical minimum center-to-center spacing 3 to 5 diameters (p. 4).
Limited to soil or very weak rock; drilled shafts are often socketed into rock (p. 5).
QA for integrity and capacity less reliable than for driven piles; spoils need disposal (p. 6).

sections.title: Construction Sequence
sections.summary: Heading for the CFA construction sequence: drilling (2.2.1) and grouting (2.2.2), the latter in five parts from the general sequence to reinforcement placement.
sections.body: Heading for the construction sequence: drilling (2.2.1) and grouting (2.2.2: general sequence, start of grouting, withdrawal of auger, grout vs. concrete, reinforcement); it has no text of its own. (p. 6)
key_points: Construction sequence: drilling (2.2.1) then grouting (2.2.2) (p. 6).

sections.title: Drilling
sections.summary: The auger flights must stay filled with soil while drilling; rotating too fast for the penetration rate makes the auger an 'Archimedes pump' that removes soil, relieves horizontal stress and causes subsidence (Figure 2.5). Only enough soil to offset auger volume and bulking should be conveyed. Drilled displacement (DD) piles displace soil laterally to avoid mining (Figure 2.6).
sections.body: The pile is drilled in one continuous operation; while advancing the auger it is essential that the flights be filled with soil so the hole stays stable. If the auger turns too rapidly relative to the rate of penetration it acts as an 'Archimedes pump' and conveys soil to the surface, reducing the horizontal stress that maintains stability; lateral movement of soil toward the hole and loss from over-excavation can cause ground subsidence and reduced confinement of nearby piles (Figure 2.5, after Fleming, 1995: top, balanced rotation and penetration with flights filled from the digging edge; bottom, slow penetration and insufficient base feed, so the auger feeds from the side with decompression). Cut soil bulks and the auger and its hollow center tube take volume, so some soil must be conveyed up, but only enough to offset the auger volume and bulking; controlling the penetration rate avoids lateral decompression, loosening and subsidence (p. 7). The proper rate may be hard to keep if the rig lacks torque and down-force, especially in mixed profiles: a low-torque rig that cannot penetrate a strong stratum at the proper rate can 'mine' the overlying weak soil to the surface. One solution is tools that displace soil laterally: drilled displacement (DD) piles, patented systems with a center pipe, an auger of larger diameter than conventional CFA (Figure 2.6) and a bulge or plug that forces soil laterally. Mining is avoided and the soil is densified with higher lateral stresses and capacity, but torque and down-force demand is greater, limiting depth and use in very firm to dense soils. Where soils are stable (cohesion, cementation, apparent cohesion above low groundwater) and piles are short, e.g., residual soil, weak limestone and cemented sands, drilling rate and mining may be neglected, but only after successful test installations and load tests confirm satisfactory results without subsidence (p. 8). (pp. 6 to 8)
key_points: Auger flights must remain filled with soil to keep the hole stable (p. 6).
Over-rotation conveys soil up ('Archimedes pump') and can cause subsidence (Figure 2.5) (p. 6).
Convey only enough soil to offset auger volume and bulking; control the penetration rate (p. 7).
Low-torque rigs in mixed profiles can mine weak soil above a strong layer (p. 7).
DD piles displace soil laterally: no mining, densified soil, but higher torque and down-force (p. 7).
Neglecting drilling rate is acceptable only after successful test installations and load tests (p. 8).

sections.title: Grouting
sections.summary: The grouting stage must begin immediately after the auger reaches the required depth: grout or concrete is pumped under pressure through a hose to the rig top and down the hollow auger stem to its base (Figure 2.7). The term grout is used for either grout or concrete.
sections.body: When drilling is complete and the auger has reached the required depth, grouting must begin immediately. Grout or concrete is pumped under pressure through a hose to the top of the rig and delivered to the base of the auger via the hollow center of the stem. The generic term grout is used in the rest of the document for grout or concrete. Figure 2.7 shows the hole at the base of the auger stem; Figure 2.8 shows grout delivered by truck to a pump near the rig. (p. 8)
key_points: Grouting must begin immediately once the auger reaches the required depth (p. 8).
Grout is pumped through the hollow auger stem to its base (Figure 2.7) (p. 8).

sections.title: General Sequence
sections.summary: General grouting sequence: lift the auger 150 to 300 mm (6 to 12 in.) and pump to expel the plug, screw back to tip elevation; pump continuously under pressure (typically up to 2 MPa, 300 psi, at the auger top) while lifting smoothly; clear spoils; clean the pile top; lower the cage into the fluid grout and tie it off.
sections.body: The general sequence: (1) at design tip elevation the auger is lifted a short distance [typically 150 to 300 mm (6 to 12 in.)] and grout is pumped under pressure to expel the plug at the base of the internal pipe; the auger is screwed back down to the original tip elevation to establish a head of grout on the auger and good bearing contact at the tip; (2) grout is pumped continuously under pressure [typically up to 2 MPa (300 psi) at the top of the auger] while the auger is lifted smoothly in one continuous operation; (3) soil is removed from the flights at the surface as the auger is lifted, so cuttings are not lifted high (safety hazard); (4) after the auger clears the surface, remaining cuttings are removed and the pile top cleared of debris and contamination; (5) the reinforcement cage is lowered into the fluid grout to the required depth and tied off at the surface. (pp. 8 to 9)
key_points: Lift 150 to 300 mm (6 to 12 in.) to expel the plug, then re-penetrate to tip elevation (p. 8).
Grout pumped continuously, typically up to 2 MPa (300 psi) at the auger top, while lifting smoothly (p. 9).
Cage lowered into fluid grout and tied off at the surface (p. 9).

sections.title: Start of Grouting
sections.summary: Grouting must start immediately at tip elevation or the auger may become stuck; rotating without penetration while waiting for grout causes mining and loss of side friction and is not recommended. Do not start drilling until enough grout is on site. Lift before blowing the plug is limited to 150 mm (6 in.) to protect end bearing.
sections.body: Grouting must begin immediately on reaching tip elevation; any delay may leave the auger stuck. Maintaining slow rotation while waiting for grout (to avoid 'hanging' the auger) leads to soil mining and degradation or loss of side friction; rotation without penetration is not recommended. The best way to avoid such problems is not to start drilling until enough concrete/grout is on site to complete the pile. After reaching tip elevation the operator typically lifts the auger about 150 mm (6 in.) and pumps under pressure to expel the plug ('clearing the bung' or 'blowing the plug'); some lift up to about 300 mm (12 in.), but the lift must be limited to 150 mm (6 in.) because a greater lift does not favor good end bearing: stress relief below the auger, a disturbed bearing surface and grout mixed with loose soil at the toe. The auger is then re-penetrated to the original tip elevation while pressure is maintained on the grout. (p. 9)
key_points: Grouting must begin immediately at tip elevation (p. 9).
Rotation without penetration is not recommended (mining, loss of side friction) (p. 9).
Do not start drilling until enough concrete/grout is on site to complete the pile (p. 9).
Lift before blowing the plug must be limited to 150 mm (6 in.) (p. 9).

sections.title: Withdrawal of Auger
sections.summary: Grouting pressure, commonly 1.0 to 1.7 MPa (150 to 250 psi) at the auger top, must exceed the overburden pressure at the auger tip and be maintained during slow, smooth withdrawal. Grout volume must be delivered continuously and monitored, with an overrun of about 15 to 20% above theoretical; pulling too fast necks the pile. Pull with no rotation or slow rotation in the drilling direction.
sections.body: Pressure is developed at the start of grouting and monitored; it is commonly 1.0 to 1.7 MPa (150 to 250 psi) at the top of the auger and must at least exceed the overburden pressure at the discharge point at the auger tip after accounting for elevation head (p. 10); it is maintained as the auger is slowly and smoothly withdrawn and replaces the soil-filled auger as lateral support. Over-rotation during drilling (excess rotation relative to depth per turn) clears the auger of soil, so grout flows up the flights, vents to the surface and pressure can no longer exceed the overburden stress. An adequate, controlled grout volume must be delivered as the auger is withdrawn to replace soil and auger; an overrun of about 15 to 20% above the theoretical pile volume should be required. Volume is measured and monitored continuously; pulling too fast for the pump makes the soil collapse inward and form a neck, and pulling fast then slowing to 'catch up' builds a series of necks and bulges. The auger is pulled with no rotation (a static condition at the base) or slow continuous rotation in the drilling direction (less risk of sticking; spreads grout from an off-center plug); rotation must be very slow so soil is not conveyed up ahead of the auger. When grout reaches the surface, the pressure is vented; the proper volume must still be delivered per increment of length and grout on the augers must not flow back into the hole with soil. The pile top is then cleared of debris and contamination; a small form is recommended (p. 10). Figure 2.9 shows how hard the pile top can be to find; Figure 2.10 shows a dipping tool removing contamination and placement of the reinforcement. (pp. 9 to 11)
key_points: Grouting pressure commonly 1.0 to 1.7 MPa (150 to 250 psi) at the auger top (p. 9).
Pressure must exceed the overburden pressure at the auger tip (p. 10).
Grout overrun of about 15 to 20% above theoretical volume should be required (p. 10).
Pulling too fast forms necks; discontinuous withdrawal forms necks and bulges (p. 10).
Withdraw with no rotation or very slow rotation in the drilling direction (p. 10).
A small form at the pile top is recommended (p. 10).

sections.title: Grout vs. Concrete
sections.summary: U.S. practice mostly uses sand/cement grout, 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi), 8 to 11 sacks per cubic yard, often with fly ash and slag (about 12 to 15% each, 24 to 30% combined); workability is measured by flow cone. Europe uses concrete with pea-gravel aggregate, about 42% sand, target slump 200 mm +/- 25 mm (8 in. +/- 1 in.).
sections.body: U.S. practice mostly uses a sand/cement grout; European practice almost exclusively concrete, which U.S. contractors are using more; both have been successful (p. 11). Grout gives fluidity and easy reinforcement installation; typical compressive strength in transportation projects is 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi); grouts are rich in cement, 8 to 11 sacks per 0.76 cubic meter (1 cubic yard); aggregate is concrete sand; a fluidifier is used as a pumping aid, retardant and shrinkage control. Fly ash and slag often replace part of the cement, typically around 12% to 15% each for a combined 24% to 30%; with fly ash alone, 25 to 70 lbs per cubic yard, 40 lbs typical. They improve workability and pumpability and reduce bleeding and shrinkage but slightly retard early strength (56-day strength may be comparable), so the mix submittal should include strength vs. time. Grout workability is measured with a flow cone (Chapter 7), not slump; retarders are not commonly used but the mix must stay fluid during rebar placement. Start drilling only when the full volume of grout is on site. Soil matters: rebar may be easy to place for up to 30 minutes in saturated clays, but dry sandy soils can dewater grout quickly, and setting-time tests may then be unreliable; retarders or anti-washout agents (viscosity-modifying admixtures, VMA) may be needed for long cages in sand; test installations and willingness to adjust the mix are important. Concrete uses pea-gravel aggregate with around 42% sand; it is cited as less costly than grout, less prone to overrun and more stable in soft ground; target slump is 200 mm +/- 25 mm (8 in. +/- 1 in.), as for wet-hole drilled shafts (p. 12). (pp. 11 to 12)
key_points: Grout strength in transportation projects typically 28 to 35 MPa (4,000 to 5,000 psi) (p. 12).
Grout: 8 to 11 sacks per cubic yard; fly ash and slag about 12 to 15% each (p. 12).
Mix submittal with fly ash/slag should include strength development vs. time (p. 12).
Grout workability by flow cone, not slump (p. 12).
Dry sandy soils can dewater grout quickly; retarders or VMA may be needed for long cages (p. 12).
Concrete: pea gravel, about 42% sand, slump 200 mm +/- 25 mm (8 in. +/- 1 in.) (p. 12).

sections.title: Reinforcement (Rebar)
sections.summary: Reinforcement goes into the fluid grout immediately after auger removal; 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft) lengths are feasible. A single full-length center bar (Figure 2.11) guides a partial-length cage and resists tension; minimum cover 75 mm (3 in.). Europe uses vibratory drive heads (Figure 2.12). CFA grout placement can only be monitored remotely by volume and pressure.
sections.body: Reinforcement is placed into the fluid grout/concrete immediately after the auger is removed; lengths of 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft) are considered feasible, depending on soil conditions, though longer has been used. Contractors often install a single full-length bar in the center (Figure 2.11) and a cage of partial-length bars around the perimeter; the full-length bar gives continuity, guides the cage and resists tension, with a wire 'football' on its end to anchor it in the grout. A minimum cover of 75 mm (3 in.) is commonly adopted. Placement is difficult if the concrete starts to set, and free-draining sand or dry soil can dewater it rapidly. In Europe a small vibratory drive head is common (Figure 2.12: a Munich project with 1-m (3-ft) piles through gravelly sand, 18-m (60-ft) machine-welded cages over the full length, concrete); vibration can cause problems with cages not securely tied or welded and segregation and bleeding if the mix is not well proportioned (p. 13). Unlike a drilled shaft, where concrete is tremied or chuted into a hole with a pre-positioned cage and access tubes for integrity testing, CFA grout placement can only be monitored remotely and indirectly by the volume delivered and pumping pressure, and the grout must stay workable for the cage to pass through; the CFA system depends on operator control during grouting and withdrawal (p. 14). (pp. 13 to 14)
key_points: Reinforcement lengths of 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft) considered feasible (p. 13).
Single full-length center bar plus partial-length perimeter cage is common (p. 13).
Minimum cover of 75 mm (3 in.) commonly adopted (p. 13).
CFA grout placement can only be monitored remotely by volume and pressure (p. 14).

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: CFA piles offer significant speed and cost advantages in favorable circumstances but pose quality-control difficulties if careful construction practices are not followed; Chapter 3 covers applications and favorable and unfavorable conditions.
sections.body: The chapter gives a general overview of CFA piles, the construction sequence and potential limitations and difficulties. CFA piles have significant advantages of speed and cost effectiveness in favorable circumstances and can pose difficulties for quality control if careful construction practices are not followed. Chapter 3 describes applications in transportation projects and favorable and unfavorable project and geotechnical conditions. (p. 14)
key_points: Speed and cost advantages in favorable conditions; quality control depends on careful practice (p. 14).
sections.applicability: Summary of CFA pile construction and its quality-control demands
